beats.text: Removing the pump handle did not end the cholera outbreak.
beats.note: Deaths were already falling. Whitehead's table shows fatal attacks dropping from 142 on 1 September to 14 on 8 September, the day the handle came off.

beats.context: On or near Broad Street in the first three days, in Soho in 1854. By the end of the outbreak the toll was 420.

beats.note: The deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump. None of the workers at the nearby brewery caught cholera, and they drank a beer allowance instead of the well water.

beats.text: The man who traced the first case had started as a doubter.
beats.note: Rev. Henry Whitehead believed in bad air until Snow's maps convinced him. He traced the outbreak to an infant at 40 Broad Street.

beats.text: The authorities still blamed bad air.
beats.note: London's Board of Health ultimately attributed the epidemic to miasma. William Farr only accepted Snow's diagnosis in 1866.

beats.text: His water test proved nothing. The pattern of the deaths made the case.
